q: The chair shows methylcyclohexane with the CH<sub>3</sub> group axial. After a ring flip, the CH<sub>3</sub> group is
c: equatorial and still on the top face; this conformer is lower in energy
equatorial and now on the bottom face; this conformer is lower in energy
still axial, because a ring flip only rotates the whole molecule
equatorial and still on the top face; this conformer is higher in energy
h: A ring flip interconverts axial and equatorial positions. Does it break any bonds, and can a group that pointed up end up pointing down?
w: A ring flip swaps every axial position for an equatorial one, but no bonds break, so each group stays on the same face (up stays up). The CH3 becomes equatorial, still on the top face, and the flipped chair is lower in energy (by about 7.3 kJ/mol) because the two 1,3-diaxial CH3/H interactions are gone.
x: Up/down (wedge/dash) cannot change without breaking a bond; the CH<sub>3</sub> stays on the top face after the flip.
A ring flip is not a rigid rotation: each carbon moves, and axial positions become equatorial.
Equatorial CH<sub>3</sub> avoids the 1,3-diaxial interactions with axial H atoms, so the flipped chair is more stable, not less.

q: The A-value of a methyl group is 7.3 kJ/mol (ΔG° for equatorial ⇌ axial). What percentage of methylcyclohexane molecules have the CH<sub>3</sub> equatorial at 25 °C?
h: Use ΔG° = −RT ln K with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin. Then convert K (equatorial : axial) into a percentage.
w: K = [equatorial]/[axial] = eΔG°/RT = e7300/(8.314 × 298) = e2.95 ≈ 19. Fraction equatorial = 19/(19 + 1) = 95%.
x: 75% corresponds to K = 3, which would need an A-value of only about 2.7 kJ/mol.
99.9% needs K ≈ 1000 (about 17 kJ/mol); that level of preference is typical of tert-butyl, not methyl.
5% is the axial fraction; the larger share is equatorial because that conformer is lower in energy.

q: Which monosubstituted cyclohexane has the largest fraction of molecules with the substituent equatorial at 25 °C?
h: Compare A-values: which group cannot avoid pointing a CH<sub>3</sub> at the axial hydrogens when it is axial?
w: The equatorial preference grows with the A-value: Br (about 2.0 kJ/mol) < CH3 (7.3) < isopropyl (9.2) < tert-butyl (about 21). tert-Butylcyclohexane is more than 99.9% equatorial and is effectively locked.
x: Isopropyl can rotate so its C–H points toward the ring, keeping its A-value (9.2 kJ/mol) far below tert-butyl's.
Methyl has an A-value of 7.3 kJ/mol, so about 5% of molecules are still axial at 25 °C.
Br has a small A-value (about 2 kJ/mol) because the long C–Br bond keeps it away from the axial H atoms.

q: The A-value of Br (about 2.0 kJ/mol) is much smaller than that of CH<sub>3</sub> (7.3 kJ/mol). Which explanation is best?
c: The C–Br bond is much longer than a C–C bond, so an axial Br sits farther from the 3- and 5-axial H atoms
Br is more electronegative than C, so it pulls electron density away from the axial H atoms and reduces their repulsion
An axial Br forms weak hydrogen bonds to the 3- and 5-axial H atoms, which offsets its steric strain
Br is so polarizable that its 1,3-diaxial interactions are attractive, so axial Br is preferred
h: A-values measure 1,3-diaxial crowding. Compare the C–Br bond length (about 1.94 Å) with a C–C bond (1.54 Å).
w: Steric strain depends on distance. The longer C–Br bond places an axial Br farther from the axial H atoms on C3 and C5, so the 1,3-diaxial interactions are weak even though the Br atom is large. A CH3 on a short C–C bond also carries three H atoms that crowd the ring.
x: Electronegativity does not reduce steric repulsion; Cl and Br have nearly equal A-values despite different electronegativities, because the larger Br atom is offset by its longer bond.
C–H bonds in cyclohexane are not hydrogen-bond donors; there is no hydrogen bonding between axial H and Br.
Br still prefers the equatorial position (its A-value is positive), so axial Br is not favored.

q: The chair conformation shown is one conformer of which compound?
h: Count ring positions between the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Then decide whether each points up or down; one axial and one equatorial alone does not decide cis or trans.
w: The CH3 groups are on carbons separated by two ring carbons on each side: a 1,4 relationship. One is axial pointing up; the other is equatorial on a carbon whose axial bond points down, so its equatorial bond tilts up. Both point up: cis-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane. (The ring-flipped chair has the same energy.)
x: In trans-1,4 one group is up and the other down, which in a chair means both axial or both equatorial; here one is axial and one equatorial.
The substituents are across the ring (1,4), not separated by a single CH<sub>2</sub> (1,3).
The substituents are 1,4, and in any case one up and one down is not what the chair shows.

q: The two chair conformations of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane are shown. Which statement is correct?
c: II is much more stable, because both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equatorial
I is more stable, because cis groups must both be axial to stay on the same face
I and II have equal energy, because each has one axial and one equatorial CH<sub>3</sub>
II is more stable only because it has less torsional strain than I
h: Identify each CH<sub>3</sub> as axial or equatorial in I and in II. In I, how close are the two axial groups to each other?
w: In I both CH3 groups are axial on the same face, 1,3 to each other: a severe CH3/CH3 1,3-diaxial interaction plus two CH3/H interactions. In II both are equatorial with no 1,3-diaxial strain. II is much more stable (both equatorial); cis-1,3 is the diequatorial-capable isomer.
x: Cis groups can both be equatorial: equatorial bonds also point up or down. In 1,3-cis both up positions are equatorial in chair II.
Equal energy (one axial, one equatorial in each chair) describes trans-1,3 or cis-1,2/cis-1,4, not cis-1,3.
Both chairs are fully staggered, so torsional strain is the same; the difference is steric 1,3-diaxial strain.

q: The chair shows one conformation of a 4-methylcyclohexanol stereoisomer. Using the A-values in the table, which chair is favored at equilibrium, and by how much?
c: Neither; both chairs have one axial group, so they are equal in energy
h: Decide which group is axial in the drawing and which will be axial after the flip. The energy difference is the difference between the two A-values.
w: In the drawing the OH is equatorial and the CH3 is axial (both on the top face, so this is the cis isomer). After the flip the CH3 becomes equatorial and the OH axial. Axial CH3 costs 7.3; axial OH costs 3.9. The ring-flipped chair is favored by 7.3 − 3.9 = 3.4 kJ/mol.
x: The chair shown has the larger group (CH<sub>3</sub>) axial, so it is the higher-energy conformer.
11.2 kJ/mol adds the two A-values; each chair has only one axial group, so the difference is 7.3 − 3.9.
Each chair has one axial group, but not the same group; the A-values differ, so the energies differ.

q: Which chair is the most stable conformation of trans-1-tert-butyl-3-methylcyclohexane?
h: First discard any chair that is not the trans compound (one group up, one down). Then, between the two chairs of the trans compound, put the larger group equatorial.
w: III and IV have both groups on the same face: they are cis-1,3, a different compound. I and II are the two chairs of the trans isomer: in I tert-butyl is axial and CH3 equatorial; in II tert-butyl is equatorial and CH3 axial. A trans-1,3 compound must have one group axial, so the bulky tert-butyl (A ≈ 21 kJ/mol) takes the equatorial site: II.
x: I puts the tert-butyl group axial (A-value about 21 kJ/mol) instead of CH<sub>3</sub> (7.3 kJ/mol), so it is much higher in energy than II.
III has both groups equatorial, but both are on the top face: that is cis-1-tert-butyl-3-methylcyclohexane, not the trans isomer.
IV has both groups on the top face (cis isomer) and both axial, the worst possible arrangement.

q: The chair conformation shown is one conformer of which compound?
h: The two Cl atoms are on adjacent carbons and both axial. Do adjacent axial bonds point to the same face or to opposite faces?
w: Axial bonds alternate up, down, up… around the ring, so axial groups on adjacent carbons point to opposite faces. One Cl is up and the other down: trans-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane in its diaxial chair. Its ring flip gives the diequatorial chair.
x: Both axial does not mean same side: on adjacent carbons one axial bond points up and the other down, which is trans.
The Cl atoms are on neighboring carbons (1,2), not separated by a CH<sub>2</sub> (1,3).
The Cl atoms are on neighboring carbons, and they point to opposite faces, so the compound is neither 1,3 nor cis.

q: Which dimethylcyclohexane can adopt a chair with both methyl groups equatorial?
h: Read each drawing as cis or trans. Then recall which cis/trans pattern lets both groups be equatorial for 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-substitution.
w: Both-equatorial is possible for trans-1,2, cis-1,3 and trans-1,4. The choices are trans-1,4 (wedge and dash), cis-1,4, cis-1,2 and trans-1,3. Only trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane qualifies: in one chair both CH3 groups are equatorial.
x: cis-1,4: in a chair one 1,4 position is axial and the other equatorial when both point up, so one CH<sub>3</sub> is always axial.
cis-1,2: adjacent groups on the same face are always one axial and one equatorial.
trans-1,3: one group up and one down on 1,3 carbons means one axial and one equatorial in either chair.

q: For which constitutional pattern of dimethylcyclohexane is the cis isomer more stable than the trans isomer?
c: For all three, the trans isomer is more stable
h: The more stable isomer is the one that can put both CH<sub>3</sub> groups equatorial. Work out which (cis or trans) allows that for each pattern.
w: Diequatorial requires trans for 1,2 and 1,4 but cis for 1,3. So cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane (diequatorial chair) is more stable than trans-1,3 (always one CH3 axial), by about 7 kJ/mol.
x: For 1,2, trans can be diequatorial, while cis always has one axial CH<sub>3</sub>; trans is more stable.
For 1,4, trans can be diequatorial, while cis always has one axial CH<sub>3</sub>; trans is more stable.
1,3 is the exception: there the cis isomer is the diequatorial one.

q: The two chairs of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane are shown. Each CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol, and a gauche CH3/CH3 interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol. What is the energy difference between the two chairs?
h: Count the 1,3-diaxial CH<sub>3</sub>/H interactions in the diaxial chair. In the diequatorial chair, are the adjacent CH<sub>3</sub> groups anti or gauche to each other?
w: Chair I is diaxial: each axial CH3 has two CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interactions, 4 × 3.8 = 15.2 kJ/mol; the axial CH3 groups are anti to each other, so no gauche term. Chair II is diequatorial: no diaxial strain, but adjacent equatorial CH3 groups are gauche (60°), 3.8 kJ/mol. Difference = 15.2 − 3.8 = 11.4 kJ/mol, favoring II.
x: 15.2 kJ/mol is the strain of the diaxial chair alone; the diequatorial chair is not strain-free because its CH<sub>3</sub> groups are gauche.
7.6 kJ/mol counts only one axial CH<sub>3</sub>; in the diaxial chair both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are axial.
3.8 kJ/mol is only the gauche term of the diequatorial chair, not the difference between the chairs.

q: Using 3.8 kJ/mol for each CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interaction and 3.8 kJ/mol for a gauche CH3/CH3 interaction, by how much is trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane more stable than the cis isomer (each in its best chair)?
h: The best chair of trans is diequatorial; any chair of cis has one axial and one equatorial CH<sub>3</sub>. Do adjacent axial/equatorial groups also have a gauche relationship?
w: trans (diequatorial): one gauche CH3/CH3 = 3.8 kJ/mol. cis (axial/equatorial): two CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interactions = 7.6 kJ/mol, plus the adjacent CH3 groups are still gauche = 3.8 kJ/mol; total 11.4. Difference = 11.4 − 3.8 = 7.6 kJ/mol in favor of trans.
x: 3.8 kJ/mol ignores the gauche interaction in cis: adjacent axial and equatorial groups are also 60° apart.
11.4 kJ/mol is the total strain of cis, not its difference from trans, which still has one gauche interaction.
The two chairs of cis are equal to each other, but cis and trans are different compounds with different strain.

q: Which property of a substituent on a cyclohexane ring is unchanged by a chair–chair ring flip?
c: Whether it points up or down (its wedge/dash sense)
Whether it is axial or equatorial
The energy of the conformer that contains it
h: A ring flip involves only rotations about C–C single bonds. What would have to happen for a substituent to move to the other face?
w: A ring flip converts every axial position to equatorial and vice versa, but because no bonds break, a group on the top face stays on the top face. The up/down (wedge/dash) sense, and therefore cis/trans relationships, never change.
x: Axial and equatorial are exactly what a ring flip interchanges.
Axial groups have 1,3-diaxial interactions and equatorial groups do not, so this count changes when the ring flips.
The energy usually changes, because groups that move from equatorial to axial pick up 1,3-diaxial strain.

q: Rank these conformations of cyclohexane from lowest to highest energy: boat, chair, half-chair, twist-boat.
h: The boat has flagpole crowding and eclipsed bonds; twisting relieves some of both. The half-chair, with several carbons nearly coplanar, is the transition state for ring flipping.
w: Chair (0, strain-free) < twist-boat (about 23 kJ/mol) < boat (about 29 kJ/mol, flagpole steric strain plus eclipsed C–H bonds) < half-chair (about 45 kJ/mol, the energy maximum on the ring-flip path). Order: chair < twist-boat < boat < half-chair.
x: The boat is higher than the twist-boat: twisting partly relieves the flagpole interaction and the eclipsing, so the boat is a local maximum between twist-boats.
The half-chair is the highest point on the ring-flip path, not the second-lowest conformation.
The chair has no angle, torsional or flagpole strain and is lower in energy than the twist-boat.

q: Which Newman projection, viewed along the C1–C2 bond, represents the diequatorial chair of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane? (C3 and C6 are the ring CH2 carbons attached to C2 and C1.)
h: In a chair, ring bonds C6–C1 and C2–C3 are gauche. Axial groups on adjacent carbons are anti; an equatorial group is anti to a ring C–C bond.
w: In every chair the two ring bonds (to C6 and C3) are gauche. Axial bonds on C1 and C2 are anti; each equatorial bond is anti to a ring bond. In I the two H atoms are anti (both axial), each CH3 is anti to a ring carbon (equatorial), and the CH3 groups are gauche: I is the diequatorial trans chair.
x: II has the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups anti to each other: both are axial. That is the diaxial chair of the trans isomer, not the diequatorial one.
III has the front CH<sub>3</sub> anti to the back H (axial) and the back CH<sub>3</sub> anti to C6 (equatorial): one axial and one equatorial, which is the cis isomer.
IV puts C6 and C3 anti to each other (180°), which is impossible in a six-membered ring, where these ring bonds are gauche.

q: The chair shows a stereoisomer of 3,5-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol. Which statement is correct?
c: The OH is trans to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the chair shown is the more stable chair
The OH is trans to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the ring-flipped chair is more stable because the OH becomes equatorial
The OH is cis to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the chair shown is the more stable chair
The OH is cis to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the ring-flipped chair is more stable because the OH becomes equatorial
h: Assign up or down to each group (an equatorial bond tilts opposite the axial bond on its carbon). In the flipped chair, which groups become axial, and are any 1,3-diaxial?
w: The OH on C1 is axial and up. The CH3 groups on C3 and C5 are equatorial; the axial bonds on C3 and C5 point up, so their equatorial bonds tilt down. The OH is up and both CH3 are down: OH trans to both CH3 groups. Ring flipping would make both CH3 groups axial on the same face, 1,3 to each other (a severe CH3/CH3 diaxial clash plus four CH3/H interactions), far worse than one axial OH. The chair shown is the more stable chair.
x: The flip moves the OH to equatorial but forces both CH<sub>3</sub> groups axial and 1,3-diaxial to each other, which costs far more than one axial OH.
The equatorial CH<sub>3</sub> groups on C3 and C5 tilt down (their axial bonds point up), so they are on the opposite face from the axial-up OH: trans, not cis.
The CH<sub>3</sub> groups are on the opposite face from the OH (trans), and the flipped chair is the less stable one.

q: Which statement about cis- and trans-decalin (bicyclo[4.4.0]decane) is correct?
c: trans-Decalin cannot undergo a chair–chair ring flip, but cis-decalin can
cis-Decalin cannot undergo a chair–chair ring flip, but trans-decalin can
cis-Decalin is more stable than trans-decalin because its ring-fusion H atoms are on the same face
In trans-decalin both rings must adopt boat conformations
h: In trans-decalin, the bonds from each fusion carbon into the second ring are both equatorial. What would a ring flip require of those bonds?
w: In trans-decalin the second ring is attached through two equatorial bonds of the first ring (trans-1,2-diequatorial). A ring flip would make both bonds axial and anti (180° apart), too far apart to be bridged by a four-carbon chain. So trans-decalin is conformationally locked, while cis-decalin (one axial, one equatorial fusion bond) flips freely.
x: It is the reverse: cis-decalin, joined through one axial and one equatorial bond, can flip, because flipping just swaps which fusion bond is axial.
trans-Decalin is the more stable isomer (by about 11 kJ/mol); cis-decalin has extra gauche interactions.
Both rings of trans-decalin are chairs; it is rigid, but in a strain-free double-chair shape.

q: In the preferred chair conformation of the compound shown, the Br atom is
c: axial, because the tert-butyl group occupies an equatorial position
equatorial, because Br is larger than a hydrogen and avoids 1,3-diaxial strain
axial half the time and equatorial half the time, because the two chairs are equal in energy
axial, because Br has a larger A-value than the tert-butyl group
h: Is this cis or trans? Then decide which group controls the conformation.
w: Both Br and tert-butyl are wedged: this is cis-1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane. In a cis-1,4 compound one group is axial and one equatorial. tert-Butyl (A ≈ 21 kJ/mol) insists on equatorial, which forces Br axial, because the tert-butyl group is equatorial. This locked axial Br is why the cis isomer undergoes E2 much faster than the trans isomer.
x: Br would prefer equatorial on its own, but in this cis-1,4 isomer the Br can be equatorial only if tert-butyl is axial, which costs far more.
The A-values differ greatly (tert-butyl about 21 vs Br about 2 kJ/mol), so the two chairs are not equal; the tert-butyl-equatorial chair dominates.
The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong: Br's A-value (about 2 kJ/mol) is much smaller than tert-butyl's.

q: A-values (kJ/mol): CH<sub>3</sub> 7.3, CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> 7.5, CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> 9.2, C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> about 21. Why does the A-value rise only slightly from methyl to isopropyl but jump sharply for tert-butyl?
c: Ethyl and isopropyl can rotate to point a C–H over the ring; axial tert-butyl must point a CH<sub>3</sub> at the 3- and 5-axial H atoms
Isopropyl is smaller than ethyl, so the two groups’ A-values nearly cancel the effect of the extra carbon
tert-Butyl is the only group that adds torsional strain to the ring C–C bonds, even when it is equatorial
Branched groups are more electron-donating, and tert-butyl donates enough to destabilize the axial C–H bonds of the ring
h: Picture each group axial and spin it about its bond to the ring. Can it always find an orientation that aims only an H toward the ring?
w: An axial group interacts mainly with the 3- and 5-axial H atoms through whatever it points toward the ring. Ethyl and isopropyl can rotate so that a small H faces the ring and the CH3 groups point outward, so their A-values stay near methyl's. tert-Butyl has three CH3 groups and no H, so one CH3 must always point at the axial H atoms, causing severe steric strain and a large A-value.
x: Isopropyl is larger than ethyl; the small change in A-value comes from rotational freedom, not size.
The jump comes from axial tert-butyl's steric clash with the 3- and 5-axial H atoms; equatorial tert-butyl is nearly strain-free.
A-values reflect steric 1,3-diaxial interactions; electron donation by alkyl groups does not explain the jump.
